claim: ISIC Revision 5 is the current endorsed global reference structure for classifying economic activities, while its formal publication is still described by UNSD as forthcoming.
assertion_scope: Foundation selection of a global economic-activity spine

support.locator: ISIC introduction and Revision 5 status paragraphs

defeaters: National implementations and datasets may still operationally use earlier editions.

claim: The exact official ISIC Revision 5 CSV imported here contains 830 nodes: 22 sections, 87 divisions, 258 groups and 463 classes.
assertion_scope: Structural completeness of isic-rev5.nodes.jsonl against one source digest

support.locator: All 830 CSV data rows; SHA-256 recorded in source registry

inference: Counts are a deterministic computation over the edition-frozen source file, not a separately quoted UNSD claim.
defeaters: A future corrected source file with a different digest requires a new import edition and review.

claim: Economic activity, product, provider, function, regulatory line and criticality must be modeled as linked classification axes rather than one inheritance tree.

support.locator: Classification inventory by statistical domain
CPC purpose and concept classified
Separate HC, HP and HF classification tables
COFOG definition as government function/purpose

inference: Because the authorities classify different units and concepts, parent-child substitution would change meaning.

claim: An official correspondence row does not by itself prove semantic identity, record-level recodability or time-series comparability.

support.locator: Definitions of within-classification and between-classification correspondence tables
Transition, backcasting and double-reporting guidance
Section 10 mapping properties and exactMatch/closeMatch semantics

inference: Separate backcasting and mapping procedures show that correspondence alone is insufficient for value-preserving recoding.

claim: National activity classifications derived from or aligned with international systems retain their own editions, detail and assignment boundaries.

support.locator: Canadian industries, comparability markers, variants and ISIC correspondence
Sections 1–2 on ISIC framework adoption and Singapore modifications
International alignment described as far as possible

claim: The digitally enabling/ICT analytical view spans manufacturing, wholesale trade, telecommunications, software, data services and repair activity codes and is narrower than the digital economy.

support.locator: Digital industries chapter, table 5.1 and surrounding limitation text

defeaters: National statistical offices can use other approximations because of data availability.

claim: Tourism industries are a cross-industry overlay derived from activities that typically produce products acquired by visitors, including partial and country-specific category extents.

support.locator: Chapter 5 and Annex 3
Purpose, structure and ISIC Revision 4 correspondence metadata

defeaters: Tourism-characteristic classification does not imply that all customers or outputs are tourism-related.

claim: Health-system analysis requires separate provider, function and financing classifications, so a general hospital industry code cannot replace the health analytical ontology.

support.locator: ICHA classification chapters
Tables A.1–A.3 for HC, HP and HF

inference: Separate authoritative axes imply that hospital activity is insufficient to encode care function and financing.

claim: Education programme level and field of study are independent cross-classification variables and neither is identical to education-provider industry.

support.locator: Section 1 definition and classification dimensions
Paragraphs 6–9 on field, level independence and hierarchy

inference: Provider industry is a third axis because ISCED assigns programmes and qualifications.

claim: SIEC provides exhaustive and mutually exclusive categories within its energy-product scope, not within the universe of energy industries, assets, flows or market roles.

support.locator: Introduction and stated SIEC scope
Chapter III classification criteria and coding system

inference: Product-scope exhaustiveness cannot establish economic-activity or asset-scope exhaustiveness.

claim: Critical-infrastructure sectors classify vital functions, assets, systems and networks and may span multiple ordinary industries.

support.locator: Critical infrastructure definition and 16-sector overview

inference: Interconnected functional sectors cannot be treated as mutually exclusive establishment activities.

claim: A complete economic-activity hierarchy does not prove complete analytical-needs coverage for every subindustry.

Multiple specialist classifications across statistical domains
